hook_text: She tried charging R12. Then R8. By mid-morning the street had taught her the one law of perfect markets.
clip_script: Market day. Forty tables down the taxi-rank street, every one piled with the same red tomatoes. A new seller sets up. She tries twelve rand a kilo when every other table asks ten. Buyers glance, take two steps, buy identical tomatoes for ten. She sells nothing. So she tries eight rand to steal the crowd — sells out by nine o'clock. Clever? No. She could already sell EVERYTHING at ten. She just donated two rand on every kilo. By mid-morning she knows the street's one law: the price is ten because the whole street made it ten, and no single table can move it. Economists call her a price taker, and her only real decision is how many kilos to bring. Even that has a rule: keep adding kilos while one more earns more than it costs — stop when the next kilo would cost more than the ten it fetches. That's the famous MR equals MC, and it's just the arithmetic of not being silly. And here's the ending the exam loves: if tomato tables start clearing pure profit, nothing stops table forty-one from arriving. More tables, more tomatoes, price slides — until sellers earn a fair return and not a cent more. Profit is the invitation. Entry is the RSVP.
visual_style: One long market street drawn in warm colours, forty identical tomato pyramids receding to the horizon; price tags flip from 12 to 8 to 10 over one table while buyers drift like a current toward the cheapest identical pile.
mood: Playful and street-smart, tightening to a crisp economic punchline.
pacing: Quick failure beats at twelve and eight, a slow settling at ten, then an accelerating tables-arriving montage to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw the whole perfect-market diagram — flat line, tick, U and rectangle — from one street story.
